title: Earth at Night: A Flickering Light Show Seen from Space
summary:
Have you ever looked at Earth from space at night? It's like a glittering spiderweb of lights. But those lights are changing—and not always how you'd expect. NASA's Black Marble satellites have been watching our planet's nighttime glow since 2014. They just released a new map showing where lights got brighter (yellow and gold) and where they dimmed (purple).

Overall, the world got 34 percent brighter! But that number hides a twist: many places actually got darker. In the United States, West Coast cities like Los Angeles brightened as more people moved there. But the East Coast dimmed, partly because cities switched to energy-saving LED lights. LEDs use less electricity, so they can make a city look less bright from space.

In China and northern India, lights surged as new buildings and roads popped up. But in Europe, many countries dimmed on purpose. France cut its light pollution by 33 percent, the UK by 22 percent, and the Netherlands by 21 percent. In 2022, Europe's lights dimmed sharply during an energy crisis caused by the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

These maps aren't just pretty—they show how humans are reshaping the night. They reveal stories of growth, conservation, and conflict. Next time you see a streetlight, think about the bigger picture it paints from space.
why_it_matters: The streetlight outside your window is part of a giant glowing web that astronauts can see – and how we use those lights changes the night sky and affects animals right near your home.

background_read: Scientists have used nighttime satellite pictures since the 1970s to see how cities grow. Brighter areas usually mean more people and more electricity being used.
Too much light at night can confuse animals. For example, baby sea turtles follow moonlight to the ocean, but bright streetlights can lead them the wrong way.
Dark-sky parks are places where lights are strictly controlled so people can see thousands of stars – something fewer and fewer kids can do from their backyards.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's Black Marble satellites, plus cities and countries around the world.
WHAT: A new worldwide map showing where nighttime lights grew brighter (yellow/gold) or dimmer (purple).
WHERE: Across the globe, from the U.S. East and West coasts to China, India, and Europe.
WHY: The lights reveal human stories – growth, energy savings, and even conflicts that forced countries to dim lights on purpose.

perspectives.description: Dimming lights saves energy and money, and helps keep the night sky dark for stargazing and wildlife.
Many bright cities waste energy and create light pollution that harms birds, insects, and even people's sleep.
The maps don't just show lights – they show how different regions balance growth, technology, and conservation.
